verses.translation_literal: And were completed the heavens and the earth and all their host.
verses.translation_dramatic: And it was finished. The heavens stood complete, the earth stood complete, and everything that fills them, every ranked and shining thing, was in its place. Nothing was left to be made. A great quiet gathered over it all.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb is passive: the heavens and earth 'were completed', and no one is named as doing it. The scene opens on a finished stage before the main actor speaks again. The KJV's opening 'Thus' is a small harmonizing bridge back to chapter 1; the Hebrew has only 'and'. (The chapter break itself is a medieval Christian addition; the Hebrew text runs straight on from the sixth day.)

The odd word is 'host' (tseva'), an army-word. In the ancient Near East the sun, moon and stars were gods or the courts of gods, and 'the host of heaven' was what neighbouring peoples worshipped. Here the host is simply part of what was made and finished. Ramban reads 'their host' as everything that fills heaven and earth, and even finds a hint of the angels in it (Ramban on Genesis 2:1). The KJV's 'all the host of them' is a stiff, word-for-word calque; the Hebrew has one suffixed noun, 'their host'.

philological_notes.note: A passive stem (Pual) of the root 'to finish, bring to completion'. It carries a sense of being brought to a full, perfect end, not just stopped. The root returns in v.2, so the reader hears the finishing twice.

'Their host': the root is the military 'army, service'. Used of the stars and heavenly beings elsewhere (Deut 4:19, 1 Kgs 22:19). Placing the host among the created things quietly demotes the divinities of neighbouring cults.

verses.translation_literal: And God completed on the day the seventh his work which he had done, and he rested on the day the seventh from all his work which he had done.
verses.translation_dramatic: On the seventh day God set down the last of his work, the work he had done, and he stopped. He rested on that seventh day, rested from all the work he had done, and the world held still around him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The hard word is 'on the seventh day he completed'. If the work was finished on day six, how can it be finished on day seven? Ancient readers felt the knot too. Rashi's answer: flesh and blood cannot know the exact moment, so must add a little of the ordinary day to the holy one, but God knows his moments and 'enters it like a hair's breadth', so it looks as if he finished on the day itself (Rashi on Genesis 2:2). Ibn Ezra reads the 'on' as 'before' and Radak reads it as the finishing being complete when the seventh day arrives. Some ancient versions (Samaritan, Septuagint, Peshitta) read 'sixth', which tidies the problem away; the Hebrew text keeps 'seventh'. The KJV's 'ended' is a faint archaism for 'completed'; 'rested' is right.

The verb 'rested' is shabbat, the root of Sabbath. The text does not say God was tired. Radak says the Torah speaks in human language, since God does not grow weary (Radak on Genesis 2:2, citing Isaiah 40:28). The sense is 'stopped, ceased'. Note too the repeated phrase 'the work which he had done', said twice, framing the verse like a closing door. The listener should hear a drumbeat of finished things, then silence.

philological_notes.note: 'He ceased, stopped.' The word means to cease work, not to be tired; it gives the Sabbath its name. Radak compares the hiphil in Exodus 12:15, 'remove leaven'.
'On the seventh day'. The numeral shares consonants with 'seven' and with 'swear, be full'; the day closes the week of seven. Ibn Ezra reads the 'on' as 'toward' / 'by' the seventh day.

verses.translation_literal: And God blessed [obj] the day the seventh, and he made it holy, for on it he rested from all his work which God created to make.
verses.translation_dramatic: And God blessed the seventh day. He lifted it out of the ordinary run of days and made it holy, set apart, his own. For on that day he rested from all the work that God had created, the work he had made.
verses.directors_commentary:
God blesses and makes holy not a thing or a person but a stretch of time, the first holy thing in the Bible. That is odd in a world where holiness belonged to places, temples and idols. Time itself is consecrated, and it is the one sacred thing no empire can capture. 'Holy' (qadash) means set apart, marked off, like a fenced field. The KJV's 'sanctified' is accurate but has hardened into church language; 'made holy' or 'set apart' is the Hebrew idea.

The last clause is awkward: 'which God created to make'. The KJV smooths it to 'created and made' (the ASV's 'created and made' does the same), turning an infinitive into a second finite verb. The Hebrew says 'created, to make': the work of creating was meant to go on being made. Rashi reads this as work that was still to be done and so doubled on the sixth day; Ibn Ezra, as the power given to things to reproduce their kind; Radak, that God made things to go on making after their kind (Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak on Genesis 2:3). Rashi, too, links the blessing and sanctifying to the manna, which fell doubled on the sixth day and not at all on the seventh (Exodus 16).

philological_notes.note: 'He made holy, set apart' (a Piel, causative-intensive). Holiness here is a status given by God to a span of time, not a mood. Radak ties it to Israel's later Sabbath observance, a sign between them and God.

'To make'. A bare infinitive after 'created': the sense is debated. Ramban lists readings: work fit to be done on the Sabbath but done early; the seeds of creatures to make their own kind; or an infinitive hanging back to 'rested from making'.

token_glosses.gloss: and he set apart as holy

verses.translation_literal: These [are] the generations of the heavens and the earth in their being created, in the day of YHWH God's making earth and heaven.
verses.translation_dramatic: This is the story of how it came to be, the heavens and the earth, from the day they were brought into being. On that day the LORD God made earth and heaven, and the telling begins again, closer to the ground.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two things change here: the heading and the divine name. 'These are the generations' (toledot) is the formula that will break the book into its family chapters (5:1; 6:9; 10:1; 11:10, and on). Here the family tree is of heaven and earth themselves, as if the cosmos had a line of descent. The KJV's 'generations' is faithful but sounds like a genealogy; 'accounts' or 'what became of' catches the sense of 'what these gave birth to'. Ibn Ezra reads the clause as 'what these brought forth' (Ibn Ezra on Genesis 2:4).

Then the divine name changes. Chapter 1 used only 'God' (Elohim), the general word for deity. From here the text writes 'YHWH Elohim', which the KJV renders 'the LORD God', printing the name in small capitals. The name YHWH is Israel's own, personal name for God. Ramban notes that until now only 'Elohim' appeared and ties this to the name's hidden meaning (Ramban on Genesis 2:4).

The order flips, too. Ch 1:1 says 'heavens and earth'; here the second half says 'earth and heaven'. The KJV flattens this by keeping 'the earth and the heavens' with articles that are not in the Hebrew. The reader should feel the camera turning from the sky down to the soil.

philological_notes.note: 'Births, descendants, what came from'. The structuring heading of Genesis. Applied to heaven and earth it means the story of what they brought forth, which fits the plant-and-man account that follows. Ibn Ezra glosses it as 'those that gave birth'.
'When they were created': a passive infinitive of 'create'. A midrash reads the letters as be-hey bera'am, 'with the letter hey he created them', a pun on the sound.
First time the personal name appears in the Bible. It joins the covenant name to the general word for God, perhaps so that readers hear that Israel's God is the same as the Maker of everything.

verses.translation_literal: And every shrub of the field not yet was in the earth, and every plant of the field not yet sprouting, for YHWH God had not caused rain on the earth, and a human none to till the ground.
verses.translation_dramatic: No bush of the field had yet stood in the land. No green blade had yet pushed up. The LORD God had not sent rain upon the earth, and there was no one to work the ground. The soil lay open, dry and waiting.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a sentence of absences: not yet, not yet, no rain, no one. The scene is a farmer's idea of desolation: a land with no rain and no worker. In ancient Israel, rain came only in the winter season and failed often, and everything rested on it. Where Egypt relied on the Nile and Mesopotamia on irrigation canals, Israel's farmers looked up. So the picture of a world before rain is a picture of a world before blessing.

What the KJV blurs is the word-play and the two plants. 'Shrub' (siach) is wild scrub; 'plant' (esev) is the cultivated grain and vegetables, the plants of the field that need a farmer. The KJV's 'plant' and 'herb' are fine, but they hide this distinction, which sets up the curse of 3:18 where Adam must eat the 'esev of the field'. Hebrew also plays on sound: adam (human) and adamah (ground), the human from the soil. The verb 'to till' (la'avod) is the same verb as 'to serve': the human is meant to serve the ground. The KJV's 'to till' is acceptable but loses that. YLT's 'to serve' keeps it.

Note 'caused rain' (himtir) is the causative: God is the one who makes it rain, not nature. In a world where Baal was the storm-god, that is a pointed claim.

philological_notes.note: 'To work, serve, till'. The root means both labour and service; the human is the ground's servant as well as its master. This echoes at 2:15, where the man is put in the garden 'to work it and to keep it'.
'Caused rain': a causative stem with God as the subject. In a land where rain was the gift of Baal in Canaanite belief, the verse insists it is YHWH who sends it.
'Shrub, bush': wild scrub of the open field, set against esev (cultivated plants). The pair covers the wild and the sown.

verses.translation_literal: And a mist would go up from the land, and would water all the face of the ground.
verses.translation_dramatic: But out of the earth itself a mist went up, soft and grey, rising again and again, and it spread its dampness over the whole face of the ground. The dry soil that had lain waiting began to darken and drink.
verses.directors_commentary:
Verse 5 ended on a lack: no rain, no one to work the ground. Verse 6 answers with a source of water that needs neither sky nor farmer. The water comes from below. For a Hebrew audience, whose crops lived or died by the autumn and winter rains, that is a picture of a world before anxiety: no storm to wait for, no sluice to dig. Rain was the gift Canaanites credited to Baal; here the water belongs to the one God and rises quietly from the earth he made.

The KJV ("But there went up a mist") reads the verse as one past event and adds a "But" the Hebrew does not have; the Hebrew begins with a plain "and." The verbs are an imperfect followed by a continuing form, which most naturally describes something that kept happening: water would rise and would water. The word 'ed is rare (its only other use is Job 36:27), so "mist" is a best guess. Onkelos renders it "cloud," Ibn Ezra compares it to smoke, and the Gaon, as Ibn Ezra reports, takes the vav as a negative: "no 'ed went up." Rashi uses the verse to picture the creation of man: just as a baker adds water before kneading the dough, the water comes first and then the man is formed.

Notice the shift of nouns: the water rises from 'eretz (land, earth) and waters 'adamah (ground, arable soil). The text is moving us to the ground from which 'adam will be taken in the next verse.

philological_notes.note: A rare word for something that rises from the earth, usually rendered 'mist' or 'vapour.' Onkelos translates 'cloud'; Ibn Ezra relates it to smoke. The meaning is uncertain, and the verse does not say whether it was rain-like or a mist from springs.
An imperfect verb that, followed by weqatal 'and would water,' points to repeated or habitual action rather than a single event. The KJV's 'there went up' flattens it to one occurrence.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH God formed [obj] the man, dust from the ground, and blew into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living being.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the LORD God bent to the ground and shaped the man out of its dust, as a potter shapes clay. He put his own mouth to the man's nostrils and breathed into him the breath of life. And the man, who was only earth, stirred, and drew breath, and was alive.
verses.directors_commentary:
The picture is a potter at his wheel. The verb 'formed' (yatsar) is the word for a potter, and 'dust' is the dry, workable earth. Mesopotamian myths made humans from clay mixed with the blood of a slain god; here there is no slain god and no servant race, only the earth and God's own breath. The man comes from the ground and is bound to it, which is the pun: the man (adam) from the ground (adamah). The KJV's 'man ... ground' loses the sound-link; try 'the human from the humus', or 'earthling from earth'.

The KJV's 'living soul' is the famous mistranslation. Hebrew nefesh does not mean an immortal soul inside a body; it means a creature, a breathing throat, a life. The same phrase is used for animals in 1:20 and 2:19. The man does not receive a soul; he becomes a living being. Note also the bodily rawness of 'blew into his nostrils': God's mouth at the man's face. Nothing softens it, and nothing should.

And the KJV's 'breathed' is gentler than 'blew' (nafach), the verb used for puffing up a fire. This is a breath that kindles.

philological_notes.note: 'He formed, shaped', the potter's verb (Jer 18). It stresses craft and care, and sets up the later 'inclination' (yetser) of the heart.
'A living being'. The root means throat, breath, life; the same phrase is used of animals (1:20; 2:19). 'Soul' in the KJV brings in a Greek idea the Hebrew does not have.
A pun: adam (the man) is from adamah (the ground), both from the root of 'red, earth-coloured'. The human carries his origin in his name.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH God planted a garden in Eden from the east, and he put there [obj] the man whom he had formed.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the LORD God planted a garden in Eden, away to the east, and there he set the man he had shaped from the dust.
verses.directors_commentary:
God turns gardener. The text gives the king's own planting: the trees are not left to nature. A walled or planted garden, in an ancient Near Eastern setting, was a royal luxury, a green park in a dry country, and the sign of a king's power to turn desert into water and shade. Here the king is God, and the first guest is the man he has formed.

'Eden' is a name, and it sounds like a Hebrew word for delight, but the name is also close to an old Mesopotamian word for steppe or plain; the text does not say which it means. The KJV's 'eastward in Eden' is a good reading of 'miqqedem', which can mean 'in the east' but also 'from of old, in the beginning', and some ancient translators took it that way. The garden is a place of settlement: God sets (literally 'puts', yasam) the man there as one sets a treasure in a safe place, a gentler verb than 'placed'.

philological_notes.note: 'From the east' or 'in the east', but the same word can mean 'from of old, aforetime'. The KJV 'eastward' follows the first; the Vulgate took the second. A real ambiguity.
A place-name, and also close to a word meaning 'delight, luxury'. Hebrew readers would hear both.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH God made sprout from the ground every tree desirable to sight and good for food, and the tree of the life in the middle of the garden, and the tree of the knowing of good and evil.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then, out of that same ground, the LORD God made trees spring up: every tree a delight to the eye and sweet to eat. And in the very middle of the garden stood the tree of life, and the tree of the knowing of good and evil.
verses.directors_commentary:
The trees come from the same ground as the man. The Hebrew keeps the word 'adamah, so the garden is built from the very soil of which 'adam was shaped. Gardens in the ancient Near East were royal things, planted by kings for pleasure and display; this is a planting by the divine king, and the man is its first guest.

The key word is nechmad, "desirable." It comes from the root of the verb "covet" in the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:17), and it returns in Genesis 3:6, where the woman sees that the tree is "desirable" to make one wise. The KJV's mild "pleasant to the sight" hides that the same word is planted here as an innocent delight and will turn there into temptation. The KJV also writes "the tree of life also in the midst of the garden": the Hebrew has only "and," so the tree of life is not an extra but the next item in the list, put in the middle of the garden with the same grammar as the rest. Notice also that the phrase "in the middle" attaches to the tree of life; the Hebrew does not say where the tree of knowing stands. Ramban reads both as central, partly because of Genesis 3:3 ("the tree that is in the middle of the garden"), but that is an inference. The KJV's "tree of knowledge" turns the Hebrew daʿat, a verbal noun, into a thing one possesses; "the knowing of good and evil" is closer, and commentators disagree whether this means moral discernment, sexual awareness, or the power of choice (Ramban, Sforno).

philological_notes.note: 'Desirable,' a passive form of the verb that means 'to desire, to covet.' The same root is the verb of the tenth commandment, and the same participle form appears in Genesis 3:6. The KJV's 'pleasant' hides this thread.
'In the middle of.' Onkelos renders 'bimtziʿuta,' 'in the midst.' Radak notes that a precious thing is placed in the middle so that everything around it acts as its wall.

'The knowing,' a noun built on the verb 'to know,' in a chain with 'good and evil.' Ibn Ezra thinks a word is missing (the knowing of knowing good and evil). Ramban takes daʿat as will or choice; Sforno as attention to what is good.

verses.translation_literal: And a river [was] going out from Eden to water the garden, and from there it divided and became four heads.
verses.translation_dramatic: A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden, and from there it parted and became four rivers, four great heads, running out into the world.
verses.directors_commentary:
Water at last, the thing missing since v.5. A single river rises in Eden, waters the garden, and then splits into four. The direction is the reverse of the real world, where small streams join into one large river. Here one source feeds the whole earth, and Eden is the head of everything. For a reader in a dry country, a never-failing river is paradise.

The Hebrew calls the four branches 'heads' (rashim), a word that could mean the beginnings or the main arms of a river. The KJV's 'four heads' keeps this but the English sounds odd, and BBE's 'four streams' loses the image of a river with a head and body. Ancient Near Eastern temples were often pictured with a spring or river flowing from the sacred centre; Eden fits that pattern.

philological_notes.note: 'Heads': the beginning of a river or its branch. 'Four heads' may mean four sources or four main channels, either way a river system flowing out from one centre.
'It parted, divided' (a passive stem): the river is split, not merged. The same root describes separations elsewhere in Genesis (2:24 is different; 10:5, 10:32 use it of peoples spreading).

verses.translation_literal: The name of the first Pishon; it the one circling [obj] all the land of the Havilah, where there the gold.
verses.translation_dramatic: The first of the four is named Pishon. It is the one that winds all the way around the land of Havilah, the land where the gold is.
verses.directors_commentary:
The narrator turns geographer and starts a tour. The text names rivers in order, and the first is the Pishon, which 'goes around' (hasoveb) the whole land of Havilah. The word is a participle with the article: 'the one circling', so the river is known by what it does. The KJV's 'compasseth' is old English for 'goes round'; it is accurate but archaic. 'Pison' is its old spelling.

Havilah is named elsewhere in Genesis (10:7, 10:29), among the sons of Cush and of Joktan, and is associated with Arabia, but the Pishon and its land cannot be located with certainty. Gold is the point: the land is rich, and the writer says so in a few words. The KJV's 'where there is gold' misses the article; the Hebrew says 'the gold', as if it were well known, the gold everyone has heard of.

philological_notes.note: 'The one that goes around, encircles'. A participle with the article, naming the river by its action. It suggests the river bends around a whole region.
A land, linked by the Bible with gold (also 10:7, 10:29; 25:18). Its location is uncertain; a root meaning 'sand' is sometimes offered.

verses.translation_literal: And the gold of that land good; there the bdellium and the stone of the onyx.
verses.translation_dramatic: The gold of that land is good, fine and pure. And there, too, are the bdellium and the onyx stone.
verses.directors_commentary:
The tour of riches continues. The gold of Havilah is 'good', the same word that God used of his creation again and again in chapter 1, here used of a metal. The KJV's 'there is bdellium and the onyx stone' leaves two unknown words as if the reader knew them.

Bdellium (bedolach) is uncertain. Radak, citing tradition, says it is a small round white stone, which is why the text does not say 'stone of' for it, in contrast to the onyx; he links it to the manna, which Numbers 11:7 says looked like bdellium (Radak on Genesis 2:12). Others take it as a fragrant resin or a pearl. Shoham, the 'onyx' of the KJV, may be onyx or carnelian; Radak says it is a large white stone, and the one on which the names of Israel's tribes were engraved on the priest's garments (Radak on Genesis 2:12). In short: the verse gives a list of precious things for the ancient listener's ear, and the point is richness, not mineralogy.

philological_notes.note: 'Bdellium', of uncertain identity: a fragrant gum-resin, or a pale round pearl-like stone. Numbers 11:7 compares manna to it by colour.
'The shoham stone': perhaps onyx or carnelian. Radak identifies it with the stones engraved with the tribes' names.

verses.translation_literal: And [the] name of the second river [is] Gihon; it [is] the one going around all [the] land of Cush.
verses.translation_dramatic: The name of the second river is Gihon, and it coils around the whole land of Cush, circling it like an arm.
verses.directors_commentary: The catalogue of four rivers reads like a travel-guide aside, and the actors should play it as a narrator who knows these waters. The Hebrew participle 'ha-sovev' means 'the one that circles', that is, keeps turning around the land, not merely 'passes by'. The KJV's 'compasseth' is faithful in sense but archaic, and its 'Ethiopia' for Kush is a translation of the Greek Septuagint tradition (Aithiopia), not of the Hebrew name, which stays Kush. Where Kush lay is disputed: Nubia, south of Egypt, or a region east of Mesopotamia tied to the Kassites. Rashi hears in the name Gihon a roaring, bursting-forth water, from the same root as 'to gore, to push'; Radak ties it to 'going out' and 'streams'. The text itself gives no map, only a river that wraps round a land.

philological_notes.note: A river name that sounds like the verb 'to burst forth, to gush'; the same name belongs to the spring of Jerusalem (1 Kings 1:33). Rashi hears a roaring, goring flood; Radak derives it from 'going out' and notes that the Jerusalem spring is called Gihon because many channels come out of it.
A participle, 'the one circling'. It describes the whole land as being ringed, not a river flowing past one point.

verses.translation_literal: And [the] name of the third river [is] Hiddekel; it [is] the one going [to the] east of Asshur. And the fourth river, it [is] Perat.
verses.translation_dramatic: The name of the third river is Hiddekel, and it runs on the eastern side of Assyria. And the fourth river — that one is the Euphrates.
verses.directors_commentary: Hiddekel is the Hebrew form of the Tigris, from the Akkadian Idiqlat; Asshur is both the city and the land of Assyria. The phrase 'qidmat Ashur' is 'east of Asshur' (Ibn Ezra reads the final ת as a replacement for the directional ה, 'toward the east of Asshur'). The KJV's 'toward the east of Assyria' follows that, but the ASV's 'in front of' preserves the other sense of 'qedem', 'front'. The fourth river is given no description at all, which tells the audience everyone knows it: Perat, the Euphrates, the great river of the Promised Land's northern boundary (Radak). Rashi remarks that Asshur and Cush did not yet exist; the text names them from the author's world. Play the verse as a speaker who points at familiar water.

philological_notes.note: The Tigris. Rashi and Radak, following Genesis Rabbah, derive it from 'sharp and swift' (chad + qal), a Hebrew folk etymology; the name itself is a borrowing from Akkadian.
'Qedem' means both 'east' and 'in front'; Ibn Ezra explains the form as a replacement of the directional ending, 'to the east of'.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH God took the man and set him to rest in [the] garden of Eden, to work it and to keep it.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the LORD God took the man in his hands and set him down to rest in the garden of Eden, to work it and to watch over it.
verses.directors_commentary: Verse 8 already put the man in the garden; this verse picks up the thread again to give him a job. The verb 'vayyanichehu' is from the root of 'rest' (noach), the same root as the name Noah: he is 'set down at rest', not merely 'put'. The KJV's 'put him' loses that note of settling, and 'dress it' for 'avad' is genteel; the verb is 'to serve, to work', the usual word for slaves and farmers and also for worship. 'Shamar' is 'to guard, to keep watch'. So the man's task is to serve the ground and to be its guard, in a world where farming is honest work, not yet a curse. Radak notes the suffix is feminine, as if it were the soil being tended; Ibn Ezra wonders from what a guard is needed, and answers: from the animals. The first human has a job before he has a rule.

philological_notes.note: Causative of 'to rest': 'and he made him rest', 'settled him'. Radak says the man was created near Eden and then placed inside.

'To serve it and to guard it'. The same pair of verbs later describes priestly duty in the sanctuary (Num 3:7-8); that is my reading, not stated by the commentators. The suffix is feminine though 'garden' is normally masculine; Ibn Ezra and Radak discuss whether it points to the garden or to the ground.

token_glosses.gloss: and he set him to rest

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH God commanded upon the man, saying: From any tree of the garden eating you shall eat.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the LORD God laid his charge upon the man, and spoke: "From every tree of the garden, eat. Eat, and you shall eat."
verses.directors_commentary:
The first command in the Bible is an invitation to eat. Before any prohibition is spoken, the man is given a table as wide as the garden. The verb is the repeated form that Hebrew uses for emphasis: an infinitive followed by the same verb in the imperfect, "eating you shall eat." The very same pattern appears in the next verse for the warning, "dying you shall die" (2:17), so the two halves of the speech rhyme: one tree is forbidden, but every other is given with full force.

The imperfect can express a command or a permission, and the translators split. The KJV and ASV take it as permission ("thou mayest freely eat"), adding "freely," which is not a separate word but their rendering of the repetition. Radak takes it as a command: for a man to keep himself alive on what is allowed to him is itself a duty, and that is why the verb is doubled; he compares "hearing you shall hear" (Deuteronomy 11:13). The English "you shall eat" can carry both senses, which is why the literal layer keeps it. Notice too the odd preposition: the Hebrew says God commanded "upon" (ʿal) the man, rather than "to" him. Ibn Ezra observes that this form usually introduces a prohibition, which already anticipates what is coming in verse 17.

philological_notes.note: An infinitive absolute followed by the imperfect of the same verb. It strengthens the verb: 'eating you shall eat,' i.e., 'eat freely' or 'you shall surely eat.' Radak reads it as a command and a mitzvah; the KJV as permission.
'He commanded upon.' Ibn Ezra notes that tzivah with ʿal normally introduces a prohibition (compare Isaiah 5:6), even though the first part of this speech is permission.

verses.translation_literal: And from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall not eat from it, for on [the] day of your eating from it, dying you shall die.
verses.translation_dramatic: But from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil — from that one you shall not eat. For on the day you eat of it, you will surely die.
verses.directors_commentary: After the wide sweep of 'every tree', the sentence narrows to one. The Hebrew sets 'you shall not eat from it' on a stressed, short phrase, and the actor should drop the voice here. 'Mot tamut', 'dying you shall die', uses the same doubled form as the permission, so the weight of the penalty is as strong as the grace of the gift. The KJV 'thou shalt surely die' is accurate, but 'in the day' hides that the Hebrew is a legal formula: Ramban compares 1 Kings 2:42, where Solomon tells Shimei that on the day he goes out he will 'surely die', and the sentence is a liability that takes effect later. So the sense is 'you will be liable to death', which Ramban takes as the fixed sentence taking effect, not immediate death on the spot. 'Knowledge of good and evil' is read in several ways: moral discernment, total knowledge, or, as Radak records, sexual knowledge; the Hebrew leaves it open. Note that the prohibition does not mention the tree of life, which Radak says was not forbidden.

philological_notes.note: Infinitive absolute with the imperfect: 'dying you shall die'. In royal legal speech this formula means a death sentence, not immediate death (Ramban cites 1 Kings 2:42).
'On the day of'; used idiomatically for 'when', 'at the time that'. Radak records a midrash reading the day as a day of God, a thousand years.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH God said: Not good [is] the man's being by himself; I will make for him a helper corresponding to him.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the LORD God said, "It is not good, this man alone. I will make him a helper, one who stands face to face with him."
verses.directors_commentary: Six times in chapter 1 God saw that it was 'good'; here for the first time something is 'not good', and the thing that is lacking is company. 'Levaddo' is 'by himself, alone', literally 'in his separateness'. The KJV's 'help meet' became a noun in English ('helpmeet') through a misreading; the Hebrew is two words, 'ezer kenegdo': a helper 'like opposite him', that is, matching, facing, corresponding. 'Ezer' does not imply inferiority: it is used of God himself as Israel's helper (my reading, and Psalm 121 uses the related verb). Rashi hears a pun in the two words: if he is worthy, a helper; if not, against him. Sforno hears the image of two pans of a balance level with one another. The actor playing God should sound like someone thinking out loud, not announcing a plan.

philological_notes.note: 'A helper corresponding to him': the second word means 'in front of, opposite, matching'. Rashi reads 'ezer' and 'kenegdo' as two outcomes (helper or opponent); Sforno reads 'kenegdo' as level like the pans of a scale.
'By himself, alone', literally 'in his separateness'. Sforno says the man alone could not achieve the goal of being in God's image if he had to attend to his own needs.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH God formed from the ground every living thing of the field and [obj] every bird of the heavens, and brought [them] to the man to see what he would call to it; and all that the man would call to it, a living creature, that [was] its name.
verses.translation_dramatic: And out of the same ground the LORD God shaped every wild creature of the field and every bird of the sky, and he led them to the man to see what he would call each one. Whatever the man named a living creature, that became its name.
verses.directors_commentary: The animals are made from the same 'adamah', the ground, as the man, so there is kinship here: the man's name, 'adam', comes from 'adamah', and the beasts share the clay. The verb 'vayyitzer' is the potter's word, as in verse 7; the KJV's 'formed' is right. Tense is the puzzle: the narrative form says 'and he formed', but chapter 1 has the animals created before the man, so some translators say 'had formed' (Radak reads it so). The Hebrew simply keeps the story going, and the scene is about naming. In the ancient Near East, naming is an act of authority and understanding: whoever names something knows its nature and rules it (Radak: 'as a servant before a master'). God hands the man that authority, 'to see' what he will do; he waits, curious, as one waits to see a child's choice. The phrase 'nefesh chayyah', 'living creature', is the same words as for the man himself in verse 7, so the man is calling to kin. The last clause is knotty; Rashi untangles it: 'every living creature that the man called by a name, that is its name'.

philological_notes.note: 'And he formed', the potter's verb of verse 7. Radak reads it as pluperfect, 'had formed', to fit Genesis 1; Rashi says birds are made from the swampy ground, from both water and earth.
'A living creature': the same phrase as for the man in verse 7. Ramban reads it as a hint that the man is looking for a creature like himself.
'To call, to name'. The man does the calling; the naming is delegated authority.

verses.translation_literal: And the man called names to all the livestock and to the bird of the heavens and to every living thing of the field; and for Adam he did not find a helper like his counterpart.
verses.translation_dramatic: So the man spoke the names, one after another: to every beast of the herds, to every bird that crosses the sky, to every living thing of the open field. And the names were given and the creatures went their ways. Yet for the man himself he found none who could stand beside him, face to face, as his match.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play this as a day of long, patient work that ends in a silence. The man is not merely labelling. In the ancient Near East, to name a thing is to take its measure and to stand over it, and the text says "called names" three times over the whole living world: the tame (the livestock), the winged (the bird of the heavens), the wild (every living thing of the field). The last sentence is the turn. He has now seen all of creation, and there is a gap in it.

Watch the grammar, because the KJV hides the actor. It says "there was not found an help meet for him", a passive that makes the lack seem to hang in the air. The Hebrew is active: lo matsa, "he did not find". The man is the one searching, and the one who comes up empty. Ibn Ezra (on 2:20) takes "for Adam" as "for himself": the same man, with the name standing where a pronoun would be, as in 1 Samuel 12:11, and he calls it far-fetched to make God the one who "did not find". Radak and Ramban give the same parallels. "Help meet" is also a KJV coinage: two words, "a helper" and "corresponding to him", that later English fused into "helpmeet" and then heard as one word for a role. The Hebrew 'ezer is not a lowly word (it is used elsewhere of God), and kenegdo means "like what is in front of him": someone he can face as an equal, who matches him. Rashi (via Bereshit Rabbah) hears it as the man noticing that each creature had a mate and he did not.

philological_notes.note: "A helper like his counterpart": 'ezer is a helper, not a subordinate; kenegdo is "as what is in front of him" (ke- "like" + neged "in front of" + "him"), a partner who stands opposite and matches. The Targums render it with a word for "support" that stands facing him (Onkelos: סמך לקבלה; Pseudo-Jonathan: סמיך כקבליה). The KJV's "help meet for him" later hardened into the single word "helpmeet".

Here the name "Adam" stands without the article, where English would say "for himself". Ibn Ezra explains this as ordinary biblical style (a name replacing the pronoun) and compares 1 Samuel 12:11, where the speaker names Samuel while speaking of himself; Radak and Ramban give the same parallels. So the sentence is about the man who searched, not about God.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH God made a deep sleep fall upon the man, and he slept; and he took one of his ribs and closed up flesh in its place.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the LORD God let a deep sleep fall on the man, and he slept. And God took one of his ribs, and closed the flesh over the place where it had been.
verses.directors_commentary: The first surgery is performed under anaesthesia, and the Hebrew gives it three beats: a sleep falls, the man sleeps, a rib is taken. 'Tardemah' is not ordinary sleep but a deep, trance-like state, the same word used when Abram sees the covenant vision (Gen 15:12); Ibn Ezra and Radak rank it as stronger than 'sheynah', which is stronger than 'tenumah' (dozing). The KJV 'rib' is fine for the single rib, but the Hebrew 'tzela' elsewhere means the 'side' of the tabernacle (Ex 26:20), and Rashi and Radak record the ancient view that 'tzelaot' here means 'sides': that the first human was a two-faced being later divided. The literal layer keeps 'ribs' and the notes keep the alternative. The Hebrew says nothing about pain or the wound; it only says God 'closed up', and the actor should play the verb tenderly. Radak says the sleep spared the man pain and, in the midrash he cites, kept him from seeing the woman's making, so that he would love her.

philological_notes.note: A deep, divinely caused sleep, stronger than ordinary sleep; Radak and Ibn Ezra give the ladder tenumah, sheynah, tardemah. Elsewhere it falls on Abram in Genesis 15:12.
'His ribs', or 'his sides'. Rashi and Radak report the view that the first human was two-faced and God divided it; tzela elsewhere means the side of the tabernacle.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH God built the rib which he had taken from the man into a woman, and brought her to the man.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the LORD God built the rib he had taken from the man into a woman, and he brought her to the man.
verses.directors_commentary: The verb is 'vayiven', 'and he built', the word for raising a house or a wall; the KJV's 'made he a woman' is flat. The woman is not moulded as the man was in verse 7 but built, and Rashi's midrash picks up the architecture: a structure wide below and narrow above, like a granary, to hold a child. The Hebrew says 'into a woman' (le-ishah): the rib becomes a woman, and Rashi compares 'Gideon made it into an ephod'. Then God 'brings her', as he brought the animals: this time the man is not asked to name her but to receive her. The scene has the feel of a father of the bride leading her in, which fits the ancient Near Eastern custom of a bride being given. That reading is mine, not the commentators'.

philological_notes.note: 'And he built'. The builder's verb, used of houses, altars and cities. Rashi hears in it the shape of a structure wide at the bottom to hold a child.

verses.translation_literal: And the man said: This one, the time, bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh! To this one it will be called woman, because from a man this one was taken.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the man spoke, and for the first time in all the world the silence broke into song. "This one — at last, this one! Bone of my bones. Flesh of my flesh." He turned the word over on his tongue as he looked at her. "She shall be called woman — for out of man she was taken, this one."
verses.directors_commentary: This is the first speech of a human being in the Bible, and it is poetry: the man has been naming animals, and none matched him; now he breaks into verse. Play it as relief and wonder, not as a lecture. Hebrew piles up the demonstrative: zot ("this one") opens the line, returns in "to this one" (lezot), and closes the verse as the final word, zot. The KJV loses the threefold zot: it has one "This" at the start and then only "she", so the man's repeated pointing, as if he were gesturing at her, disappears. Haphaam ("this time") says "at last, this time", after the animals that did not fit; KJV's "now" is vague. "Bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh" is covenant language for kinship (Laban and Jacob, Gen 29:14; the tribes and David, 2 Sam 5:1), not only anatomy; the man recognizes family. The wordplay ish / ishah (man / woman) is the point of the verse: the man names her in a pun that the Hebrew hears and English can only echo with "man" and "woman". Rashi notes the pun as proof that the world was created in the holy tongue. Note also that the man names her "woman", not yet "Eve"; that comes in 3:20. Before this verse he is called ha-adam, "the earthling", from adamah, soil; only now, with a woman beside him, does he speak of himself as ish.

philological_notes.note: "The time", that is, "this time", with the article: at last, this once. Radak reads it against the first presentation of the animals, when the man found no partner; this time he does. Rashi, citing the Talmud, reads it as a sign that the man had looked among the animals before.

"Woman", set against ish, "man" (word 13), as a sound-play. Ibn Ezra and Radak discuss the doubled shin that stands in for the yod of ish and note that the form avoids confusion with ishah "his wife".
A kinship formula. The literal sense is "bone from my bones": she comes from his own body, so she is his own.

token_glosses.gloss: the time, this time at last
to this one, for this one

verses.translation_literal: Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother and cleaves to his wife, and they become one flesh.
verses.translation_dramatic: And that is why a man leaves his father and his mother and clings to his wife, and the two of them become one flesh.
verses.directors_commentary: The narrator steps out of the garden and speaks to the audience: 'therefore', 'al ken', the formula for explaining a custom of the present by an event of the past. The KJV's 'shall leave' makes it a command; the verbs are imperfect and mean 'a man leaves', as a regular habit, not 'shall'. The sentence is striking in its world: in the ancient Near East, a wife normally joined her husband's family, and the man stayed on his father's land; here the man is the one who leaves. Radak says this means the man sets up house apart from his parents without ceasing to honour them. 'Davaq' is 'to cling, to stick', the word for glue and for loyalty; the KJV's 'cleave' now means both 'stick' and 'split', which obscures it for the modern ear. 'One flesh' means one kin: Ramban links it to the expression 'she'er basar' and to the fact that, unlike animals, the man holds to one woman; Rashi reads it as the child, in whom their flesh is made one. The rabbis (Sanhedrin 58, cited by Rashi and Radak) take the verse as the root of the laws of forbidden unions.

philological_notes.note: 'And he clings', the verb for glue or attachment, and also for covenant loyalty (Deut 10:20). It is the opposite of 'leaves'.
'Into one flesh'. Rashi reads it as the child formed from both; Ramban rejects this because animals also have young, and reads it as the man's attachment to his wife as to his own kin.

verses.translation_literal: And they were, the two of them, naked, the man and his wife, and they were not ashamed of themselves.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the two of them stood together, the man and his wife, with nothing on them, and neither felt any shame.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play this as a quiet statement of fact, not a nudge. The verse closes the scene and sets the baseline that the next chapter will break. The KJV is nearly right, and the one thing it loses is the word's second life: 'arummim, "naked", is spelled with the same consonants as 'arum, "shrewd" or "cunning", the very word that opens chapter 3 for the serpent. In the Hebrew ear the verse ends on a sound that the next verse picks up again. (That link is my own reading of the consonants. Targum Pseudo-Jonathan seems to hear a related sound, since where Onkelos has "naked" it has "wise".)

The verb is the other thing to notice: yitboshashu is a reflexive form, "they did not feel shame before one another, or in themselves", not simply a lack of embarrassment. Rashi (Bereshit Rabbah) says they did not yet know modesty, because they did not yet know good and evil. Radak says they had not eaten from the tree and had not yet known desire, so those parts of the body were as ordinary to them as any other. Sforno says all their limbs served the will of their Maker alone. In the ancient world, to be seen naked was the mark of a prisoner or a slave and a source of public humiliation; so this verse says their condition is the opposite of that, a state of complete ease in each other's eyes. Ibn Ezra notes that 'arummim is a plain adjective, as in Job 22:6, "you strip the clothes of the naked", and that some take 'arum in Proverbs 22:3 as the same word.

philological_notes.note: "Naked", plural adjective with the doubled mem. Ibn Ezra takes it as an adjective of state and compares Job 22:6, adding that some read Proverbs 22:3, 'arum ra'ah ra'ah, "the shrewd one sees evil", as the same word. Onkelos renders "naked" (ערטילאין); Targum Pseudo-Jonathan renders it "wise" (חכימין). Whether the Targum is hearing the pun with the serpent's 'arum in 3:1 is my inference.

A reflexive form of the root meaning "to be ashamed": "they did not feel shame before themselves or one another". Ibn Ezra says it comes from boshet (shame), with a hidden weak letter between the first two, and that the last letter is doubled as in yitbonan (Job 11:11); he adds that the vowel under the last shin is long because the verse ends here. Radak and Sforno explain the absence of shame as a state before desire and knowledge of good and evil.

events.title: God completes his work and rests on the seventh day
events.narrative_summary: The heavens, the earth and all their host are finished. On the seventh day God ends his work and rests, and he blesses that day and makes it holy because he rested on it.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Day 7 of the creation week follows day 6 (1:31, 'the sixth day') directly: anchored on the END of evt.gen_1.day6_land_life with no offset, so it begins at the evening that closes day 6 (the Hebrew day runs sunset to sunset), and lasts one day (2:2-3). Margin 0, as for the days of Gen 1: the text counts the days without gaps. Rashi, Sforno and Radak debate whether God 'finished' at the very start of the day or at its end; I keep the whole day as the span. Tier DAY_SEQUENCE: days are counted.

events.title: The LORD God forms the man from dust and breathes life into him
events.narrative_summary: Before any plant of the field had sprung up and before the LORD God had sent rain, with no man to till the ground, a mist watered the ground. The LORD God formed the man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The text gives no clock. This retells the sixth day (1:26-27), so I anchor on the START of evt.gen_1.day6_humankind, with duration 30 minutes and a margin of 3 hours. DAY_SEQUENCE because the scene falls under the counted day 6, not because an hour is given. The 'before the plants' of 2:5 is a state, not a dating.

events.title: God plants a garden in Eden with its trees and river
events.narrative_summary: The LORD God plants a garden in Eden, in the east, and makes every pleasant tree grow, with the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in its middle. A river flows from Eden to water it and divides into four heads: Pishon, Gihon, Tigris and Euphrates.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The narrative order puts the planting after the forming of the man and before he is placed there (2:8, 'the man whom he had formed'), so I anchor on the END of the forming with no offset; 1 hour and a margin of 1 hour are estimates, not text. Ibn Ezra reads the trees of the garden as sprouting when the other trees did (2:9), which would put the planting earlier; I keep the narrative order. DAY_SEQUENCE as a scene of day 6.

events.title: God puts the man in the garden to till and keep it
events.narrative_summary: The LORD God takes the man and sets him in the garden of Eden to work it and to keep it.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows the planting directly (2:15); anchor END of evt.gen_2.garden_planted, no offset, 10 minutes. Margin 1 hour for the estimate. DAY_SEQUENCE as a scene of day 6.

events.title: God allows every tree but forbids the tree of knowledge
events.narrative_summary: The LORD God commands the man that he may eat freely from every tree of the garden, but not from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, for on the day he eats of it he will surely die.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: A continuous scene after the man is placed (2:15-16); anchor END of evt.gen_2.man_placed, no offset, 10 minutes. 'In the day you eat' (2:17) is the term of the warning, not a date of this event. DAY_SEQUENCE as a scene of day 6.

events.title: God says it is not good for the man to be alone
events.narrative_summary: The LORD God says that it is not good for the man to be alone, and that he will make him a helper corresponding to him.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: A speech with no time word (2:18), placed after the command in narrative order; anchor END of evt.gen_2.command_trees, no offset, 5 minutes. DAY_SEQUENCE as a scene of day 6.

events.title: The man names the animals and finds no counterpart
events.narrative_summary: The LORD God forms the beasts of the field and the birds of the sky and brings them to the man to see what he will call them. The man gives names to all of them, but for the man no helper corresponding to him is found.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Narrative order after 2:18; anchor END of evt.gen_2.alone_decision, no offset. Naming every kind of cattle, bird and beast takes hours; I take 3 hours with a margin of 1 hour. The text states no duration. The animals' own making is day 5-6 (Gen 1), so only the bringing is dated here. DAY_SEQUENCE as a scene of day 6.

events.title: God builds the woman from the man's rib
events.narrative_summary: The LORD God causes a deep sleep to fall on the man, takes one of his ribs and closes the flesh in its place. He builds the rib into a woman and brings her to the man.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows the failed search (2:20-21); anchor END of evt.gen_2.animals_named, no offset. A deep sleep and the operation: I estimate 2 hours with a margin of 1 hour; not in the text. DAY_SEQUENCE as a scene of day 6.

events.title: The man greets the woman, and they are naked and unashamed
events.narrative_summary: The man says, 'This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man.' The text adds that a man therefore leaves his father and mother and clings to his wife, and that the two were naked and not ashamed.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Immediately after she is brought (2:22-23); anchor END of evt.gen_2.woman_formed, no offset, 5 minutes for the speech. Verse 24 is the narrator's comment and 2:25 a state, so both ride on this scene. DAY_SEQUENCE as a scene of day 6.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: God's resolve, 'I will make him a helper' (2:18), is carried out when he builds the woman from the rib (2:22).
Because no helper corresponding to the man was found among the animals (2:20), God puts him to sleep and makes the woman (2:21).
The planted garden is the place where God puts the man he has formed (2:8, 2:15).
The man speaks when God brings the woman to him (2:22-23).

entities.canonical_name: Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil
entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew ʿēṣ hadaʿat ṭôb wārāʿ; 'good and evil' probably means a complete range of knowledge or the ability to judge.
entities.summary_bio: A tree in the garden. The LORD God forbids the man to eat from it, warning that on the day he eats he will surely die.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew ʿēṣ haḥayyîm, 'tree of the life'.
entities.summary_bio: A tree the LORD God causes to grow in the middle of the garden. This chapter does not say what it does, and it is not forbidden to the man.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew kûš; the name of a land south of Egypt, rendered 'Ethiopia' in older English versions.
entities.summary_bio: The land encircled by the Gihon according to Genesis 2:13. Whether this is Nubia or a nearer region is debated.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'delight' or 'luxuriance' (Hebrew ʿēden); some link it to Akkadian edinu, 'steppe'.
entities.summary_bio: The region in the east where the LORD God plants his garden. A river rises in it and divides into four heads.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew pərāt, from Akkadian purattu; the meaning is uncertain.
entities.summary_bio: The fourth river of Eden, named without further description because it was well known.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew gan-ʿēden, 'garden in Eden' or 'garden of delight'.
entities.summary_bio: The garden the LORD God plants eastward in Eden, with every pleasant tree, the tree of life and the tree of knowledge at its centre. The man is placed there to till and keep it, and the woman is built there.
The second river of Eden, said to encircle the whole land of Cush. It is not the same as the Gihon spring at Jerusalem, though they share the name.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew ḥăwîlâ; the meaning is uncertain, possibly 'sandy land'.
entities.summary_bio: A land encircled by the Pishon, known for good gold, bdellium and onyx. It is likely a different place from the later Havilah of the sons of Ishmael, though the name is the same.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'gushing' or 'spreading' (from the root pûš); not certain.
entities.summary_bio: The first of the four rivers that branch from the river of Eden. It encircles the whole land of Havilah, where there is good gold.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew ḥiddeqel, from Akkadian idiqlat, itself of older origin.
entities.summary_bio: The third river of Eden, which flows east of Assyria.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew ʾādām, 'human, man', wordplay on ʾădāmâ, 'ground', the stuff he is made from.
entities.summary_bio: The first human, formed by the LORD God from the dust of the ground and given the breath of life. He is placed in the garden of Eden to till and keep it, receives the command about the trees, names the animals, and receives the woman built from his rib.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew ʾiššâ, 'woman'; the man explains the name by wordplay on ʾîš, 'man', from whom she was taken.
entities.summary_bio: The first woman, built by the LORD God from a rib of the man and brought to him. The man greets her as bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh, and the two live naked and unashamed. She is not yet given a personal name in this chapter.

components.evidence_explanation: Gen 2:18: God says it is not good for the man to be alone. Ends in 2:22 when the woman is brought to him.

components.label_value: Living in the garden of Eden
components.evidence_explanation: Gen 2:15: God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden.
Gen 2:7: the man became a living creature after God breathed the breath of life into his nostrils.

components.label_value: Tiller and keeper of the garden
components.evidence_explanation: Gen 2:15: he was put there to till it and to keep it.
Gen 2:25: they were both naked and were not ashamed.
Gen 2:22–24: God brings the woman to the man, and 2:25 calls her his wife.
Gen 2:17: God commands the man not to eat from it, on pain of death.
Gen 2:22–25: she is brought to the man and called his wife.
Gen 2:22: God builds the woman and brings her to the man; she appears as a living person from then on.
Gen 2:25: both were naked and were not ashamed.
Gen 2:2 says God ceased on the seventh day from all the work he had done.

systems.name: Divine formation of living beings
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Mesopotamian and Egyptian texts also tell of gods shaping humans from clay or on a potter's wheel (Atrahasis, Khnum). Genesis 2 presents the LORD forming the man like a potter, and then breathing life into him.
rules_and_mechanics: The material is drawn from the ground or from a body already made.
God shapes it by hand, so the verbs are those of a craftsman: form, build.
Life comes by God's breath or act, as in the nostrils of the man.
The animals and the woman, once formed, are brought to the man (2:19, 2:22).

systems.name: Marriage
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Marriage in the ancient Near East was normally arranged between families, with the bride moving to the husband's household. Genesis 2:24 gives an origin story in which the man leaves his parents' house and joins himself to his wife.
rules_and_mechanics: The man leaves his father and mother.
The two become one flesh, a bond of kinship, as the man says: bone of my bones, flesh of my flesh.

systems.name: Naming by a human
systems.ancient_near_east_context: In the ancient Near East a name expressed the nature of a thing, and naming expressed authority over it, as when a king renamed a vassal. Here the man names the animals.
rules_and_mechanics: God brings the creatures to the man to see what he will call them.
Whatever the man calls a creature is its name.
The act shows the man's authority and his search for a counterpart.

systems.name: Sanctifying the seventh day
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Rest and festival days tied to the moon or the calendar were known elsewhere in the region, but a recurring seventh day set apart by the creator as holy is distinctive to Israel. In Genesis the day is blessed and made holy before any law is given.
rules_and_mechanics: God finishes his work by the seventh day and ceases from it.
God blesses the day and sets it apart as holy.
The reason given is that on this day he rested from all his work.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God forms the wild animals and birds from the ground and brings them to the man.
system_instances.significance_note: Sets up the search for a counterpart and shows that none of the animals is one.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The man gives names to all the livestock, birds and wild animals but finds no counterpart among them.
system_instances.significance_note: Shows the man's authority and his need for someone like himself.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The man greets the woman as bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh, and the narrator adds that a man leaves his parents to join his wife.
system_instances.significance_note: Gives the origin of marriage as a bond of kinship, in place of the earlier loneliness.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD God shapes the man from the dust of the ground and breathes life into his nostrils, and he becomes a living being.
system_instances.significance_note: Ties the man to the ground by name and to God by breath.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God finishes his work, rests on the seventh day, blesses the day and makes it holy.
system_instances.significance_note: Sets time apart as holy and ends the creation account on rest rather than on a further act.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God allows the man every tree of the garden but forbids the tree of knowledge of good and evil, on pain of death.
system_instances.significance_note: The only limit placed on the man; it sets up the test of the next chapter.

system_instances.outcome_summary: God puts the man into a deep sleep, takes a rib, closes the flesh, builds the rib into a woman and brings her to him.
system_instances.significance_note: Gives the woman the same substance as the man, which he recognises in the next verse.

edges.description: The man gives names to the livestock, birds and wild animals.
The man says she shall be called woman, because she was taken from man.
God brings the woman to the man.
God builds the rib taken from the man into a woman.
God allows the man every tree but forbids the tree of knowledge, on pain of death.
The LORD God forms the man from the dust of the ground and breathes life into him.
God takes the man and puts him in the garden of Eden to till and keep it.
